pairs.rationale: Both concern material contributions for the saints in Jerusalem. Romans names Macedonia and Achaia's pleasure in contributing for the poor; Corinthians directs this Church as the Galatian Churches were directed.

Both name the first day of the week in community practice. Corinthians directs personal setting aside for the collection; Acts narrates an assembly for breaking bread. The activities and occasion remain distinct.

Both connect a gift's transport with approved or appointed traveling representatives. Corinthians here proposes letters and Jerusalem delivery; the other account describes a brother chosen by the Churches. No unnamed messenger is identified without evidence.

They will go with me refers to the approved gift-carriers described in the preceding plan. Paul's own participation is conditional, while the carriers and Jerusalem destination belong to the stated proposal.

Both discuss a visit to Corinth and a Macedonian itinerary. The other letter recalls a plan to visit before and after Macedonia; this letter proposes coming after passing through Macedonia. The plans are not silently made identical.

The following explanation says Paul wants more than a passing visit and hopes to remain for some time if the Lord permits. It clarifies the tentative extended or winter stay without turning perhaps into an accomplished visit.
Both condition future action on the Lord's will. James's general instruction corresponds to Paul's hope of an extended visit if permitted, without establishing a fixed itinerary.

Acts narrates Paul's work in Ephesus, including synagogue teaching and later daily reasoning in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. This supplies a specific ministry setting for remaining there, without deriving the Pentecost deadline or an exact letter date from Acts.

Both use an opened door for gospel ministry. The other letter locates its door in Troas and in the Lord; this passage concerns the Ephesian setting and also mentions many opponents. The locations and circumstances remain distinct.

Both describe Timothy's participation in gospel work for a community. Brother and God's fellow worker there corresponds to his working the Lord's work here; the two proposed or narrated visits are not identified as one mission.

The instruction that no one despise Timothy has a specific counterpart in the instruction not to let anyone despise his youth. Youth is explicit in Timothy's letter, not supplied as the stated reason for every Corinthian reaction.

The earlier discussion identifies Apollos as a servant through whom the Corinthians believed and as the one who watered. This gives the named brother's ministry context without supplying the reason he does not wish to visit now or a date for his opportunity.
Both urge steadfastness in faith. Philippians describes standing in one spirit and striving together for gospel faith; Corinthians combines standing firm with vigilance, courage and strength.
Both give love an encompassing place in conduct. Colossians calls it the bond of completeness above the other virtues; Corinthians directs that everything among the recipients be done in love.
The earlier statement names the same household of Stephanas as baptized by Paul. Here its firstfruits-of-Achaia and service descriptions add particular information about that household.

Both concern a community's response to laboring ministers. Corinthians urges submission to these servants and all coworkers and laborers; Thessalonians requests recognition and high regard in love, also naming leadership and admonition. The different directives remain distinct.

Both describe others supplying what was lacking from a community's service. Philippians identifies Epaphroditus as the community's messenger and minister to Paul and describes his risk; Corinthians names Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus. The persons and circumstances remain distinct.

Both describe refreshment received through another believer's ministry. Philemon speaks of the saints' hearts refreshed; Corinthians names my spirit and yours and urges recognition of the people involved.

Both explicitly name Aquila and Prisca and a Church in their house. Romans sends a greeting to them; Corinthians transmits their greeting. The direction differs, and no unprinted street address or exact date is supplied.
Both give the instruction to greet one another with a holy kiss, accompanied by community greetings. Romans names all Christ's Churches; Corinthians names all the brothers.
Both explicitly mark Paul's greeting as in his own hand. Thessalonians also calls it a sign in every letter; the comparison does not infer the handwriting of every earlier part of this letter.

Both use an accursed declaration. Corinthians attaches it to not loving the Lord; Galatians attaches it to a contrary gospel. The different stated grounds and Corinthians' Our Lord, come remain distinct.

Both close with the Lord Jesus' grace directed to the recipients. The other blessing also names God's love and the Holy Spirit's fellowship. The actual Greek-based final13:13 unit is retained rather than inventing13:14.

Paul's love for the addressed community is explicit in both letters. The other account describes writing through tears to make that love known; this letter ends by placing his love with all of them in Christ Jesus.
